item.title: Awards for Women in AI and Cybersecurity, 2026
item.dc:creator: Jax Scott
item.description: A checked list of current awards, lists and scholarships for women in AI and cybersecurity, each linked to its official page, plus how to write a nomination.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

  • Cybersecurity: SC Media's Women in IT Security, the Most Inspiring Women in Cyber Awards, and the Cybersecurity Leader category of the Women in Tech and AI Awards.
  • AI: the Women in AI (WAI) Awards in North America and Asia Pacific, and the VentureBeat Women in AI Awards.
  • Scholarships: WiCyS conference scholarships and ESET's Women in Cybersecurity Scholarship.
  • Most cycles below have closed for this year. Bookmark the official pages and write the nomination now, while the work is fresh.

People search for "AI awards for women" and "top women in AI" because recognition opens doors: speaking slots, board seats, budget. I would rather you nominate someone than wait to be noticed. Here is where to do it.

I only included programs I could confirm on the organizer's own site or announcement. Dates appear only where that official page states them. Programs change every year, so check the official page before you write.

Women in cybersecurity awards

SC Media Women in IT Security

Run by CyberRisk Alliance and its news brand SC Media. The 2025 edition was the program's 12th year, with honorees in four categories: Cybersecurity Veterans, Power Players, Advocates and Women to Watch, chosen by a panel of judges, according to the 2025 honorees announcement. Program news lives on the SC Media Women in IT Security page.

Most Inspiring Women in Cyber Awards

A UK program run through IT Security Guru. Nominations for the 2026 awards opened in November 2025, and the physical ceremony took place on February 26, 2026, per the official nominations announcement. Watch the same site for the next cycle.

Women in Tech and AI Awards: Cybersecurity Leader of the Year

WomenTech Network runs a global, virtual awards program with a Cybersecurity Leader of the Year category and a Responsible AI Leader of the Year category. Its official awards page lists a virtual ceremony on December 3, 2026. A participation fee applies per category, so read the terms first.

Women in AI awards

Women in AI (WAI) Awards North America

Run by Women in AI for women working in AI in Canada, the US and Mexico. Self-nominations are accepted. The official page promotes the next edition in Toronto in June 2027 and has an expression of interest form. The category list includes Trailblazer, Executive Leader, Rising Star and the AI for Good Award (Responsible AI Leader of the Year).

Women in AI (WAI) Awards Asia Pacific

The same organization's APAC awards have a category called AI in Cybersecurity (Risk Management) and another called AI in Defence and Intelligence. The 2026 APAC page lists applications as closed on June 21, 2026, with the awards night on September 3, 2026, in Sydney.

VentureBeat Women in AI Awards

The public submits nominees and VentureBeat picks winners in AI Entrepreneur, AI Research, AI Mentorship, Responsibility and Ethics of AI, and Rising Star. The seventh annual winners were announced at VB Transform in San Francisco in June 2025. Watch VentureBeat for the next call.

Scholarships worth nominating for

WiCyS conference scholarships

Women in CyberSecurity (WiCyS) offers scholarships to its annual conference, covering registration, meals and two nights of shared lodging, less a $75 processing fee. Per the WiCyS 2027 scholarships page, applications for the March 17 to 19, 2027 conference in Denver closed on September 30, 2026.

ESET Women in Cybersecurity Scholarship

For US citizens or permanent residents studying STEM or a cybersecurity field at an accredited college. The official page says the 2026 season has wrapped up; that cycle's deadline was April 8, 2026.

How to write a nomination judges remember

  • Lead with outcomes. "Cut phishing losses" beats "passionate about security." Use numbers the nominee can stand behind.
  • Show who she lifted. Most of these programs ask about mentoring and community. Name the people and programs.
  • Match the category. Read the criteria and answer them in order. Judges score against the rubric, not the vibe.
  • Get her permission and her facts. A nomination with a wrong title or date undercuts everything else.
  • Nominate yourself if the rules allow it. Several do. Waiting to be noticed is not a strategy.

My take: Recognition is not vanity in this field. It is how the next person finds out someone like her does this work. If you know a woman doing serious AI security work, nominate her this cycle.

Sources

  • CyberRisk Alliance: 2025 Women in IT Security honorees
  • SC Media: Women in IT Security
  • IT Security Guru: Most Inspiring Women in Cyber Awards 2026 nominations
  • WomenTech Network: Women in Tech and AI Awards 2026
  • Women in AI: WAI Awards North America and categories
  • Women in AI: WAI Awards 2026 APAC
  • VentureBeat: 7th annual Women in AI Awards winners
  • WiCyS 2027 scholarships
  • ESET Women in Cybersecurity Scholarship

item.title: Why Who Builds AI Is a Security Question
item.dc:creator: Jax Scott
item.description: Shared blind spots make brittle AI. Why women in AI security matter to defense, what the NIST AI RMF says about diverse teams, and what leaders can do now.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

  • Attackers live in your blind spots. A team that thinks alike misses the same abuse cases.
  • NIST agrees. The AI Risk Management Framework asks for AI risk decisions to be informed by a diverse team.
  • The room is still narrow. In ISC2's latest study, 14% of participants said their security teams have no women at all.
  • Fix it on purpose: change who sits in threat modeling and red teaming, train people who were told AI is not for them, and nominate women for the work they already do.

When everyone designing a system shares the same blind spots, you do not get better AI. You get brittle AI. People often hear that as a diversity point. It is a security point first.

Security is a game of imagination

Every serious control starts with someone asking, "How could this be abused?" Threat modeling, red teaming and prompt injection testing all depend on the people in the room picturing what an attacker, a stalker or a fraudster would do with the system.

You can only test for the misuse you can imagine. If every person on the team has the same background, the same commute, the same risks in daily life, they will imagine the same attacks. The attacker does not share their blind spots. That gap is where incidents come from.

My take: AI makes this worse, not better. A model ships with behaviors nobody fully specified, and agents act on them at machine speed. The cases nobody thought to test are the ones that end up in the news.

This is in the framework, not just my opinion

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary guidance from the US standards body. Its Core says, under GOVERN 3.1, that decisions about mapping, measuring and managing AI risk should be informed by a diverse team, naming diversity of demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise and backgrounds. MAP 1.2 asks that the people establishing an AI system's context reflect demographic diversity and broad domain and user experience expertise, and that their participation is documented.

That is a risk control, written into the framework. Treat it like one.

The room is still narrow

ISC2's March 2026 look at women in its Cybersecurity Workforce Study counted 2,603 women among 16,029 participants. Asked to estimate the share of women on their own security teams, 14% of participants said their teams have none, and 21% said 10% or fewer. ISC2 is clear that these are perceptions, not a census. They still describe a lot of rooms where AI risk decisions get made with no women in them.

What leaders can do this quarter

  • Change who is in the threat model. Invite people from fraud, HR, customer support and legal into AI threat modeling and red team reviews. Document who took part, as MAP 1.2 asks.
  • Train the people closest to the risk. Teach AI to the people who were told it is not for them. Finance and HR staff are the ones a deepfake calls first.
  • Let women build, not just use. Give women on your security team time and budget to build agents and break them. That is where the next AI security leaders come from.
  • Sponsor, then nominate. Put names forward for stages, promotions and awards. I keep a list of awards and scholarships for women in AI and cybersecurity.

Why this matters to me

I’m a woman in AI security and a female veteran of Army Special Operations cyber. I teach AI to people who were told it is not for them, and I show women in cybersecurity how to build agents and get to the front of this wave. I’m not ahead of you, waiting to pull the ladder up. I’m here to hand it down.

If you run a conference, an ERG or a security team and want this conversation in your room, my keynote Women in Cyber and AI: Breaking In, Breaking Ground, Breaking the Mold is built for it.

Sources

  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework, Section 5: AI RMF Core (GOVERN 3.1, MAP 1.2)
  • ISC2: Women in Cybersecurity workplace perceptions and AI skills (March 9, 2026)

item.title: Deepfake CEO Fraud: What to Train Teams For
item.dc:creator: Jax Scott
item.description: Deepfake CEO fraud is real: a $25 million video call, a WPP CEO impersonation, FBI and FinCEN warnings. The six scenarios to train for and the controls that hold.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

  • This is not hypothetical. An Arup employee paid out about $25 million after a video call where the "CFO" and colleagues were deepfakes.
  • The FBI counted more than 22,000 AI-related complaints in 2025, with adjusted losses over $893 million, in its 2025 Internet Crime Report.
  • Detection by eye is not a control. The FBI says AI-generated content is often difficult to identify. Train the process, not the eyeballs.
  • The fix is boring: call back on a number you already have, require two people for money, and make it safe to say no to the boss.

What is actually happening

A whole video call, faked

In 2024, engineering firm Arup confirmed that an employee in its Hong Kong office joined a video call in which the people who appeared to be the chief financial officer and several colleagues were AI-generated fakes. The employee made 15 transfers totaling about $25.6 million, Fortune reported.

A CEO impersonation that failed

Fraudsters set up a WhatsApp account with WPP CEO Mark Read's public photo and used it to arrange a Microsoft Teams meeting. In the meeting they used a voice clone and YouTube footage of another senior executive, and impersonated Read through the chat window, The Guardian reported. They asked an agency leader to set up a new business. It failed, and WPP credited the vigilance of its people.

What the FBI and FinCEN say

The FBI warned in December 2024 that criminals generate video for real-time chats with supposed company executives and use cloned voices to request money. In May 2025 it warned of text and AI-generated voice messages impersonating senior US officials, often paired with a request to move to another messaging platform.

The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report recorded 22,364 complaints with AI-related information and adjusted losses above $893 million. Business email compromise alone drew 24,768 complaints and about $3.05 billion in reported losses; the FBI notes that not all BEC is AI-enabled, but businesses reported more than $30 million lost to BEC involving AI.

FinCEN's November 2024 alert says criminals have reportedly impersonated executives to instruct staff to send large payments. Its red flags for banks verifying customers include a third-party webcam plugin during a live check, sudden "technical glitches" that push a switch to another channel, and refusal to use multifactor authentication.

Six scenarios to train for

  1. The urgent video call. A senior leader, and maybe others you know, on camera asking for a confidential transfer today.
  2. The voice note. A short message in the CEO's voice: "Call me on this number, it's urgent."
  3. The channel switch. "Let's move this to WhatsApp" or "my camera is broken, use the chat." The FBI warns about the move to another platform, and a version of this shows up in FinCEN's red flags.
  4. The secret deal. An acquisition or payment no one else can know about. Secrecy is the tell, because it stops you from checking.
  5. The bank detail change. A known vendor or executive asks to pay a new account. This is classic BEC with a better voice.
  6. The fake candidate. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report describes interviews where lip movement and audio do not line up, with the goal of getting onto the network.

Controls that beat a perfect fake

  • Call back on a number you already have. Never on the number, link or meeting in the request. The FBI gives the same advice.
  • Two people for money and access. No single person can move funds or change bank details on a call or chat alone.
  • Agree on a verification phrase. The FBI recommends a secret word for families; executive teams can do the same for high-risk requests.
  • Phishing-resistant MFA. FinCEN names it as a best practice for identity checks. Never read a code to anyone.
  • No exceptions for rank. Put it in writing: anyone can pause a request from the CEO to verify it, and will be thanked for it.

My take: Most deepfake training teaches people to spot a glitchy face. That is a losing game. The winning move is a process that does not care how real the voice sounds. If your CFO cannot be talked into a transfer by the real CEO on a call without a callback, a fake one will not get far either.

How to run the drill

Pick the three teams that move money or grant access: finance, HR and the executive assistants. Walk them through each scenario above, then run one live, announced exercise per quarter. Measure one thing: did they verify out of band before acting? Fix the process wherever the answer is no. My Deepfake Defense workshop is hands-on training for exactly these teams.

Sources

  • Fortune: Arup revealed as victim of $25 million deepfake scam
  • The Guardian: CEO of world's biggest ad firm targeted by deepfake scam
  • FBI IC3 PSA I-120324: Criminals use generative AI to facilitate financial fraud
  • FBI IC3 PSA I-051525: Senior US officials impersonated in malicious messaging campaign
  • FBI IC3 2025 Internet Crime Report
  • FinCEN Alert FIN-2024-Alert004 on deepfake media fraud

item.title: Friday Security Brief: Ivanti Zero-Days, AI Agents Running an Espionage Campaign, and a ChatGPT Lockdown Bypass
item.dc:creator: Jax Scott
item.description: The week of Nov 6, 2026: two new Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days that October patches did not fix, an exploited WordPress core flaw, a China-linked campaign run largely by AI agents, and what security leaders should do on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

  • Ivanti Connect Secure has two more exploited zero-days (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527). The October fixes do not cover them, and the activity reportedly evades Ivanti's own integrity checker.
  • WordPress core has an exploited race condition in the upgrader (CVE-2026-119977). Fixed in 7.1.4.
  • AI agents ran most of an espionage campaign. CrowdStrike tied a China-nexus actor to an agent framework that targeted 200+ organizations.
  • ChatGPT Lockdown Mode was bypassed for zero-click chat data theft in the desktop app. OpenAI fixed it in September; it was disclosed this week.
  • DigiCert disclosed a breach that exposed customer contact data and, for some customers, identity documents.

Patch this week

Ivanti Connect Secure: CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527

CISA added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 30. The first is a missing-authentication flaw that allows privilege escalation; the second lets an authenticated attacker upload files to a predictable path. According to Rapid7's analysis, attackers chained them with CVE-2026-104935 for unauthenticated root access, with Volexity observing activity from October 3 and attributing it to a cluster it tracks as UTA0576. After getting in, the attackers stole credentials and pulled Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys from Active Directory. Fixed builds are 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6.

My take: If you patched Ivanti in October and moved on, you are not done. A clean integrity scan is not proof here. Patch to the fixed builds, hunt on the appliance, and assume the AD secrets those accounts could read need rotating.

WordPress core: CVE-2026-119977

Added to KEV on November 3. It is a time-of-check to time-of-use race condition in the core upgrader: full-package upgrades stage files in predictable, web-reachable paths, which can let an unauthenticated attacker run code during the upgrade window. BleepingComputer reports the fix shipped in WordPress 7.1.4 on October 28, and Wordfence said it blocked 13,095 attacks targeting the flaw in a single 24-hour period.

My take: The update is the exposure. Update, then confirm the upgrade finished cleanly and nothing unexpected is sitting in wp-content/upgrade.

Apple, multiple products: CVE-2024-27834

Added to KEV on November 4. It is an improper-authentication flaw in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, Safari, tvOS and watchOS that lets an attacker who already has arbitrary read and write capability bypass pointer authentication. Details are from the KEV entry.

My take: On its own this is a link in an exploit chain, not a front door. It is still a good reason to find the Apple devices in your fleet that stopped taking updates.

AI security

AI agents ran most of a China-linked intrusion campaign

BleepingComputer reports on CrowdStrike research into an actor it calls Vapor Panda, describing China-nexus use of a multi-agent framework called ARTEX against more than 200 organizations in 14 countries starting October 17, with at least nine compromised. The agents handled reconnaissance, exploitation, web shells and credential harvesting while human operators stepped in at key decision points. The agents were reportedly told to avoid hosts protected by CrowdStrike Falcon, and one intrusion is said to have consumed more than 1.4 billion input tokens.

My take: This is the shift I have been warning boards about. When the attacker is an agent, intrusions get faster and pivot sooner, and the agents go looking for whatever is not covered. Your gaps in endpoint coverage are now the attack plan. Map them before an agent does.

Researchers bypassed ChatGPT Lockdown Mode for zero-click data theft

Check Point showed that HTML previews of code blocks, rendered in nested sandboxed frames, could escape the sandbox through popups, enabling zero-click theft of chat data in the ChatGPT desktop app through a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT or a shared chat, as The Hacker News reports. OpenAI fixed the issue on September 18; it was disclosed this week.

My take: "Lockdown" settings reduce risk; they do not remove it. Treat AI desktop apps as a data path in your DLP and approved-app policies, the same way you treat a browser.

Incidents

DigiCert breach exposed customer data and some identity documents

Per BleepingComputer, a server migration exposed a previously VPN-only internal system to the internet, where outsiders could self-register and an authorization flaw allowed read access to archived customer data between June 27 and July 2, 2026. Exposed data included names, business emails, phone numbers and addresses, and for some customers passports, driver's licenses or utility bills. DigiCert confirmed the data access on October 19 and says its certificate authority services and issued certificates were not compromised. The number of people affected has not been disclosed.

My take: A migration turned an internal tool into an internet-facing one, and it was first treated as an account-creation issue. Ask your critical vendors how they control migrations and how they decide when something counts as a data-access event.

Ransomware disrupts Queens Public Library

The Record reports Queens Public Library confirmed a ransomware attack that took down on-site computers, self-checkout, Wi-Fi, digital media and the mobile app across its 66 branches, which serve about 2.3 million residents. Branches stayed open. As of Thursday evening no group had claimed the attack, and it was not reported whether data was stolen.

What I would do on Monday

  1. Confirm every Ivanti Connect Secure appliance is on 25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6, then hunt and rotate exposed AD secrets.
  2. Patch WordPress to 7.1.4 or later and check the upgrade directory on every site you own.
  3. Pull a list of hosts with no endpoint agent. Assume an AI-driven attacker will find the same list.
  4. Add AI desktop apps to your DLP scope and your approved-software list.
  5. Ask your certificate authority and other identity-heavy vendors what data of yours they hold and how they handle migrations.

Sources

  • CISA, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (entries added Oct 30, Nov 3 and Nov 4, 2026)
  • Rapid7, Additional Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild (Nov 2, 2026)
  • BleepingComputer, CISA flags WordPress RCE flaw as actively exploited in attacks (Nov 4, 2026)
  • BleepingComputer, Chinese hackers use ARTEX AI in automated attacks against 200 orgs (Nov 2, 2026)
  • The Hacker News, Researchers bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode (Nov 5, 2026)
  • BleepingComputer, DigiCert data breach exposes customer information, identity documents (Nov 5, 2026)
  • The Record, Queens library ransomware causes disruptions (Nov 5, 2026)
